rows.title: Is anybody using it, and is it answering

panels.title: People using it
panels.description: Distinct people who made a request in the last fifteen minutes. THE PANEL TO READ BESIDE A LATENCY GRAPH. Nobody files a ticket about a slow page - they stop opening it - and request rate cannot tell that from a quiet week, because one person refreshing a dashboard outnumbers ten people doing a day's work. Latency rising while this falls, over the same week, is one event rather than two.

panels.title: Requests answered
panels.description: By status class. A rise in 4xx without 5xx is usually authorization, or a browser that has got ahead of a deployment; a rise in both is the service.

panels.title: Requests failing
panels.description: 5xx as a share of all traffic. Zero is the normal reading, and it is drawn as a line at zero rather than as an empty panel on purpose: a blank graph during an incident is indistinguishable from a broken one.

panels.title: Queue depth
panels.description: Jobs outstanding, by state. Deep is not the same as stuck - a busy queue is deep too - so read it beside the panel on its right, which is what tells them apart.

panels.title: Oldest job still waiting
panels.description: THE ONE TO ALERT ON. In a queue that is moving this stays flat however deep the backlog gets, because work leaves as fast as it arrives. In a stalled one it climbs in real time, minute for minute. Depth cannot make that distinction and this can.

panels.title: Throughput
panels.description: Bytes per second, split by whether they crossed the wire. `saved` is content a dedupe or a server-side mount meant nobody had to move - the number that justifies this system existing - and it is kept separate because adding the two together would report bandwidth nobody used.

panels.title: Slowest endpoints (p95)
panels.description: The five slowest route templates. Open the API dashboard to find out why one of them is here.

panels.title: Jobs failing
panels.description: Terminal failures per second, by error class. The class is the actionable part: `auth` is a credential nobody rotated, `transient` is a registry having a bad day, `digest_mismatch` is corruption. Retries are not counted here - see the transfers dashboard.

panels.title: Is anything being scraped
panels.description: One line per target. A dashboard that has stopped updating looks exactly like a system that has stopped doing anything, and this is what tells those two apart. A gap here means every graph above is stale, not that the estate is quiet.
